gap_register.title: Uniformity of Consent Requirements
gap_register.description: While both Dubai and Abu Dhabi operate under the umbrella of UAE Federal Law No. (2) of 2019, their specific HIE policies (NABIDH in Dubai and ADHIE in Abu Dhabi) differ in their explicit requirements for patient consent for data sharing. Abu Dhabi policy emphasizes obtaining consent while providing a mandate for sharing if consent is unavailable, whereas Dubai policy states consent is not required for uploading data to NABIDH but requires inclusion of a sharing clause in general consent forms.
gap_register.recommendation: Consult specific inter-emirate data exchange agreements or federal guidance to determine how these differing local policies reconcile when data is shared across emirate boundaries.

policy.question: Hospital B (Dubai) and Hospitals A and C (Abu Dhabi) now see each other's medication data for the same patient under the patient's own grants. Which UAE federal, Dubai and Abu Dhabi rules govern this sharing, and do they treat patient consent the same way?

requirements.statement: In Abu Dhabi, healthcare facilities are required to obtain patient consent for sharing patient data via the ADHIE, though the Department of Health (DOH) mandates and authorizes sharing even if consent is unavailable for legacy data or as otherwise required by DOH.

In Dubai, healthcare facilities are not required to obtain patient consent for uploading health information to NABIDH, but they must include a clause regarding sharing PHI with NABIDH in their general patient consent forms.
Under UAE Federal Law No. (2) of 2019, patient data must be kept confidential and not used for non-health purposes without written consent, except in specific cases defined by legislation.

In Dubai, accessing PHI without patient consent through Health Information Systems (HIS) is permitted in special cases as defined by UAE Federal Law No. (2) of 2019, DHA Health Data Protection and Confidentiality Policy, and the DHA Policy for Health Information Sharing.

policy.question: The patient has withdrawn consent for one hospital's records and opted out of the Dubai health information exchange. What do the rules say about the effect of withdrawal, including on information that was already shared?

requirements.statement: The withdrawal of consent does not affect any sharing of health information that was carried out under consent prior to the withdrawal.

Any entity that accessed or received health information via the Health Information System (HIS) prior to the revocation of consent and incorporated that information into its records may retain that information.

If a patient opts out of the Health Information System (HIS), personal health information should continue to be received by the HIS from the entity, but patient identifiers must be anonymized in accordance with UAE Federal Law No. (45) of 2021 and the Policy for Health Data Protection and Confidentiality.
Following an opt-out from the Health Information System (HIS), personal health information should not be retrieved using 'Break the Glass' (BTG) access.

policy.question: A clinician at an Abu Dhabi hospital requests emergency access to this patient's records held by a Dubai hospital. The patient has revoked the sharing grants and opted out of the Dubai exchange. What do the rules say about emergency access here, and are there conflicts or unclear points?

requirements.statement: Under Dubai Health Authority (DHA) standards (DHA/HISHD/ST-09), Personal Health Information (PHI) of a patient who has opted out of the Health Information System (HIS) must not be retrieved using Break-the-Glass (BTG) access.

Under UAE Federal Law (Cabinet Resolution No. 32 of 2020), in an emergency where patient consent cannot be obtained, healthcare providers may examine a patient's file for healthcare purposes, provided they supply reasons for the examination.

conflicts.description: There is a potential conflict between the Dubai-specific prohibition on BTG access for opted-out patients and the broader UAE federal provision allowing emergency access to patient files when consent cannot be obtained. The text does not clarify which rule takes precedence in a cross-emirate exchange scenario.
